items.title: Sakana AI Releases Namazu Small, a 30B Model Built on Nemotron 3 Nano
items.content:
Sakana AI has announced Sakana Namazu Small, a 30-billion-parameter reasoning model built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano. The Japan-based lab ran continued pretraining and post-training in-house, starting from Nemotron 3 Nano’s pretrained base. Sakana AI team states that the result beats NVIDIA’s 120B Nemotron 3 Super on its 25-benchmark average. 



TL;DR




Size: 30B total parameters, 3B active (labeled 30B-A3B in Sakana’s chart). Context length: Not disclosed.



Runs on: Hardware not disclosed. Sakana says it is small enough for your own environment. The Nemotron 3 Nano base was designed for DGX Spark, H100 and B200 GPUs.



Performance: 60.1 average on 25 benchmarks, ahead of Nemotron 3 Super (56.2) and Nano (50.2). Self-reported.



Best: BrowseComp 73.5, about 2x Nemotron 3 Super’s 36.1.



Worst: SimpleQA Verified 6.8, below Nemotron 3 Nano (9.1) and Super (18.1).




What is Sakana Namazu Small?



Sakana Namazu Small is a 30B-A3B reasoning model from Sakana AI, tuned for web research and long-document QA. “Sakana Namazu” names models Sakana builds on open models and finishes with its own post-training. The larger Sakana Namazu is based on Kimi K2.6. Namazu Small is the compact member of that family.



Sakana AI targets 3 kinds of work: everyday conversation, research with web search, and reading long documents. It was developed as a reasoning model. It organizes the information it needs and reasons step by step toward an answer.



How was Namazu Small trained?



Sakana started from the pretrained base of Nemotron 3 Nano, not NVIDIA’s post-trained release. It then applied continued pretraining and post-training techniques built for this release. These sit on top of methods Sakana developed for the original Sakana Namazu.



The base architecture matters for deployment. Nemotron 3 Nano is a hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model. NVIDIA lists it at 30B total and 3B active parameters, with context up to 1M tokens. 



How does Namazu Small perform on benchmarks?



Sakana compared it against 2 NVIDIA models, both post-trained by NVIDIA. These are Nemotron 3 Nano (30B-A3B) and Nemotron 3 Super (120B-A12B). The suite spans 25 benchmarks in 3 groups. All scores are self-reported by Sakana.



Benchmark groupNamazu Small (30B-A3B)Nemotron 3 Super (120B-A12B)Nemotron 3 Nano (30B-A3B)Overall (25 benchmarks)60.156.250.2Web search (9)59.954.649.3Context grounding and instruction following (8)67.156.453.9Knowledge (8)53.257.847.6



Where does it win?



Web research is the standout. On BrowseComp, Namazu Small scores 73.5 versus 36.1 for Super and 29.3 for Nano. On DeepSearchQA it reaches 84.3, against 65.4 for Super.



Grounded long-document answering also jumps. LLM-jp LongBench rises to 86.0, versus 67.0 for the Nano baseline. FaithEval reaches 78.3 versus 59.1 for Super. LongBench-Cite hits 80.2 and ALCE reaches 60.2, both citation-focused tasks.



Where does it fall short?



Closed-book knowledge is the weak spot. On SimpleQA Verified it scores 6.8, below Super (18.1) and Nano (9.1). Japanese SimpleQA lands at 8.0, versus 24.9 for Super. HealthBench drops to 40.6, under Nano’s 47.5. Sakana itself says tasks using only internal knowledge did not improve much.



Per benchmark, Namazu Small beats Super on 13 of 25 tests. It beats Nano on 22 of 25.

items.content:
OCRia-nano-1 Technical report · Blog post · LiteParse · OCRia-1 · ParseBench OCRia-nano-1 is an 8.1M-parameter model pipeline for document parsing on CPU from LlamaIndex .
It pairs a detector–recognizer OCR stack with LayoutNet, a joint table and layout model, and it runs inside LiteParse , the open-source local document parser. Its models are distilled
from OCRia-1 , our 4B document VLM, with 1/500th of its parameters. Accuracy: 59.2 on ParseBench-2 , ahead of the CPU parsers Indra (55.1) and
Marker (52.5). It lifts LiteParse from 48.7 with Tesseract. See Benchmarks . Speed: 27.8 pages per second on 16 vCPUs, 426 ms per page on one core, twice as fast as LiteParse with Tesseract. Tables and layout: LayoutNet finds tables (rows, columns, spanning header cells) and classifies layout blocks
(headings, lists, captions, page headers and footers) on scanned and born-digital pages. Scripts: a router sends each text line to one of four recognizers: Latin, CJK, right-to-left (Arabic, Hebrew),
and a world-script model for about 17 more scripts. CPU runtime, everywhere LiteParse runs: the CLI, Python and Node.js on Linux, macOS and Windows, and the browser and
edge runtimes through WebAssembly. These are the model files LiteParse runs; they are not a standalone model with its own inference script. LiteParse
renders the page, runs the detector, router and recognizers, merges the OCR text with the PDF text layer, runs
LayoutNet, and writes Markdown or JSON with bounding boxes. Use them through LiteParse (see Quickstart ). Examples Text lines detected on scanned pages, colored by the recognizer the router picked for each line: LayoutNet's layout blocks on two multi-column pages, from the PDF text layer alone: Quickstart Install LiteParse ( pip install liteparse , npm i -g @llamaindex/liteparse or cargo install liteparse ), then pull
the models once. lit models pull downloads this repository's files and ONNX Runtime and checks every file against
its pinned sha256; after that, OCRia-nano-1 is LiteParse's OCR backend by default. lit models pull ocria-nano # once: models + ONNX Runtime (60-75 MB) lit parse scan.pdf --format markdown # OCR, tables and layout with OCRia-nano-1 lit parse scan.pdf --ocr-backend tesseract # force Tesseract for one run Python from liteparse import LiteParse, models

models.pull( "ocria-nano" )
result = LiteParse(ocr_backend= "ocria-nano" , output_format= "markdown" ).parse( "scan.pdf" ) print (result.text) Node.js import { LiteParse , models } from "@llamaindex/liteparse" ;

models. pull ( "ocria-nano" ); const result = await new LiteParse ({ ocrBackend : "ocria-nano" , outputFormat : "markdown" }). parse ( "scan.pdf" ); console . log (result. text ); Browser and edge (WebAssembly) WASM and edge runtimes fully support OCRia-nano. You can also control which models download to minimize download sizes. import init, { LiteParse , OcriaNano } from "@llamaindex/liteparse-wasm" ; await init (); const ocria = await OcriaNano . fromUrl (); // or { scripts: ["latin"], layout: false } for 1.5 MB of models const parser = LiteParse . withOcriaNano ({ ocrEnabled : true , outputFormat : "markdown" }, ocria); const result = await parser. parse (pdfBytes); Input PDFs, images and Office documents (through LiteParse's conversion) Pages render at 250 DPI for OCR by default ( --dpi changes it). Language detection is automatic, the router in OCRia-nano picks a recognizer per line. Output LiteParse's Markdown, text or JSON. With OCRia-nano-1: Content How it is written Tables Markdown tables, or HTML with colspan / rowspan for spanning cells Headings and lists Markdown headings and list items, from LayoutNet's layout classes Page headers and footers removed from the Markdown by default, kept with --keep-headers-footers Layout blocks with --extract-blocks , JSON blocks (heading, paragraph, table, figure, ...) with boxes and links to their text items Words and lines JSON text items with bounding boxes and OCR confidence How it works Model File Role Parameters Line detector det.onnx segmentation map of text lines, depthwise-separable 0.08M Script router router.onnx picks a recognizer per line crop, and detects upside-down lines 0.04M Latin recognizer rec_latin.onnx CTC, int8, supports 791 characters 0.80M World-script recognizer rec_world.onnx CTC, about 17 scripts 0.98M RTL recognizer rec_rtl.onnx CTC, Arabic and Hebrew 0.71M CJK recognizer rec_cjk.onnx CTC, Chinese, Japanese and Korean 1.27M LayoutNet tablenet.bin / tablenet.onnx 6-layer transformer over text units with a CNN image branch: table, row, column, cell and layout-block relations, 13 layout classes 4.27M Total 8.1M The OCR stack is 3.9M parameters. LiteParse runs the ONNX models on ONNX Runtime natively and on tract in WebAssembly. Benchmarks Results from the technical report . Every local system runs on
the same 16-vCPU machine and throughput is measured on 300 random ParseBench pages, with one worker per core. System (CPU) ParseBench-2 OmniParseBench ParseBe

items.title: AI solved the hardest problem in maths – is there anything it can’t do?
items.content:
Alzheimer’s disease, involving amyloid plaques in the brain, will be tough for AI to solveJUAN GAERTNER/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY



The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI. Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths. The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced.



	
		
			Read more
			Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis
		
	



We see this messaging in claims that AI can “solve X”, where X is any field of human endeavour you care to name. Biology is a big one. “Cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness – these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei while promoting the company’s recent initial public offering. “I think one day maybe we can cure all disease with the help of AI,” said Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, last year, adding that this could be “within the next decade or so”.



This phenomenon isn’t new: I call it “physicist brain”, after the propensity for physicists to wade into areas outside their expertise and declare simple solutions. More broadly, it is called Nobel disease, after the many Nobel prizewinners who have gone on to make, shall we say, less evidenced-backed claims. In general, there is a tendency to think that if an intelligent person is good at one thing, they are good at many other things that require intelligence. What is different now is that trillion-dollar companies and large swathes of the global economy now depend on this being true of artificial intelligence.

	
		
							
					Advertisement				
						
				
			
		
	





To be clear, I think we must now admit that AI is better at solving open mathematical problems than any human, and that this has happened faster than anyone ever expected. When I first saw the news in September that the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by OpenAI, I felt stunned. We had entered a new world. With the announcement of the Riemann hypothesis proof this week, I felt sick and had to go and have a lie-down. These were intellectual Everests I have marvelled at since my teenage years, conquered by a machine far sooner than anyone expected. You may have read my recent piece forecasting the future in 2096 – an early draft had a line, later removed, about three Millennium Prize Problems being solved by AI in the 2030s. We’ve had two this year alone.



But maths isn’t biology. Yes, we have seen advances like AlphaFold, Deepmind’s AI that can predict the structure of proteins, but this is biology at its most mathematical, a computational puzzle. True advances in biology and medicine require studying cells, animals and people, all of which can be frustratingly illogical and uncooperative. Amodei admitted as much in 2024, writing that “the main challenges with directly applying intelligence to biology are data, the speed of the physical world, and intrinsic complexity”. You can imagine mitigations here – AI-directed robotic labs, for example – but it doesn’t seem like we should expect massive speed leaps in capability comparable to those seen in mathematics. There isn’t an easy way to confirm that a biological discovery is correct, in the manner that the computer code Lean allows for mathematics.



Worse still are claims that AI will “solve climate change”. For Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, this came as a throwaway comment in a 2024 essay: “Although it will happen incrementally, astounding triumphs – fixing the climate, establishing a space colony, and the discovery of all of physics – will eventually become commonplace.”



But we already know the solution to climate change: reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero and the warming will stop. The blockers to doing so, as demonstrated by the recent failure of the COP31 climate summit, are political, not technological. Even if AI were to produce a blueprint for a perfectly functioning nuclear fusion reactor tomorrow, we would still have to build thousands of them across the globe in the next decade or so to avoid the most catastrophic warming effects. In the past decade, we have built 60 nuclear fission reactors, a technology we understand far better than an as-yet-mythical fusion power plant. Again, you can see how AI might offer some improvements, but not enough to counteract our fossil fuel use.



It is important for me to have some humility here, because one thing AI’s breakthroughs in mathematics this year has underlined for me is the need to change my mind when the evidence changes. I started that process with the early signs of AI progress in maths, but didn’t update my beliefs fast enough – though, to be fair to myself, neither did almost everyone else, including leading mathematicians such as Terence Tao, who, just weeks ago, said he didn’t expect the Riemann hypothesis to be solved by AI until 2050.



For that reason, I am on the lookout for early signs that AI success in biology is shifting. That could include an AI-designed drug proving useful in people – for example, Rentosertib, a leading candidate, is now undergoing a phase III trial as a treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a type of lung disease. The trial is expected to conclude in 2029, so we’re talking years of wait for any results. If the drug succeeds, that doesn’t necessarily provide a way for any other AI drug candidates to succeed, and the painfully slow process of molecule selection, animal testing and human trials is still hard to speed up.



If I’m forced to make a prediction, I can fairly confidently state that we will see yet more advances in AI maths in 2027. I also expect that we will see some completely unexpected results in other fields as well. But solving biology? Ending climate change? Defeating disease? These still feel, for now, like science fiction.



	
		
			Read more
			AI refutes 30-year-old mathematical assumption in computer science
		
	



Further AI reading




AI maths has become a spectator sport, thanks to a website dedicated to tracking agents attempting to solve the P vs NP problem, one of the remaining huge open problems in mathematics (see my explanation of it here). I don’t expect this approach to work – the models being used here are consumer ones, rather than the internal frontier models the AI firms have used for the big maths results so far.



As if to illustrate this, both OpenAI and Anthropic have released, with little fanfare, solutions to the VP vs VNP problem. This is a lesser version of the P vs NP problem, and doesn’t necessarily help us get any closer to solving its big brother.



And speaking of internal models, Axios reports that both Anthropic and OpenAI employees are concerned that their internal models are so powerful that they can’t safely be released. Take this with a big pinch of salt – Anthropic said the same about its Mythos model due to its cybersecurity abilities, then later released its Fable model, which is essentially just Mythos with some added guardrails. And don’t forget that, way back in the mists of 2019, OpenAI said that GPT-2 would be too dangerous to release. Today, you can run far more capable models on a smartphone, and no one finds that dangerous.



Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after a mere 11 days away following a scandal about his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy. For a reminder of why Nvidia is so important to the AI industry, see my previous column.



A UN conference has failed to agree to a ban on autonomous weapons, as my colleague Matthew Sparkes predicted last week.

As if to illustrate this, both OpenAI and Anthropic have released, with little fanfare, solutions to the VP vs VNP problem. This is a lesser version of the P vs NP problem, and doesn’t necessarily help us get any closer to solving its big brother.

And speaking of internal models, Axios reports that both Anthropic and OpenAI employees are concerned that their internal models are so powerful that they can’t safely be released. Take this with a big pinch of salt – Anthropic said the same about its Mythos model due to its cybersecurity abilities, then later released its Fable model, which is essentially just Mythos with some added guardrails. And don’t forget that, way back in the mists of 2019, OpenAI said that GPT-2 would be too dangerous to release. Today, you can run far more capable models on a smartphone, and no one finds that dangerous.

Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after a mere 11 days away following a scandal about his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy. For a reminder of why Nvidia is so important to the AI industry, see my previous column.

A UN conference has failed to agree to a ban on autonomous weapons, as my colleague Matthew Sparkes predicted last week.

items.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
items.content: Open video on YouTube ↗Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use.  Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue, the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation.  By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph.  Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. Sculptor started as a tool loop. Now it's a coding agent. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings.  The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows.  Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together. Jump to the Sculptor discussion →Most companies post-train too early For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks.  Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million. Jump to the post-training discussion →$1,500 to score every company in the world Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market.  Jeff puts a good enrichment budget at $1 to $10 per qualified lead and $10 to $100 per booked call. He thinks qualification itself is close to solved. Models have been scoring about as high as they can on Clay’s evals for roughly a year. Just about any model from the past year can pull a company’s latest funding round. Frontier models still matter for deep prospecting research and for orchestration, where Jeff says the best plays can be ten to a hundred times as effective as an average one. Jump to the Jev discussion →Customers hate the model selector Customers complain when they see Clay’s model selector. They can’t check the evals for their use case every time a new model ships, and they shouldn’t have to. Clay is about to launch an automatic router that picks a model for each task. There’s no fancy branding. Finding Apple’s CEO is a very different job from finding the CEO of an obscure local company.  The selector isn’t going away. Agency owners and power users still want control. Everyone else just wants to get on with their work. Clay has to earn their trust before they’ll leave it on auto. Jump to the model routing discussion →No Temporal, no LangGraph Clay built most of its agent stack itself. It uses BullMQ to keep agent jobs running, Postgres and ClickHouse for product data, and Snowflake for analytics. Jeff isn’t sure how BullMQ will hold up if usage grows another tenfold, but it’s held up so far. Clay recently shipped 25 to 30 new integrations. Contracts and testing took longer than the engineering work.  Where Clay did run into trouble was scale. People run an agent per row, so if someone starts a run on a table of 50,000 companies, inference demand spikes all at once. Clay brought in LangSmith to see what was happening. The team also built a way to throttle requests and to pause and resume work when a provider goes down or starts rate-limiting. The harder part is keeping things fair. Someone running a workflow for ten people still needs it to run when an enterprise customer is enriching a million rows. Jump to the infrastructure discussion →Built for every agent, not just Clay's Clay plans to ship a sandboxed agent that’s free to use any of Clay’s tools and building blocks. Jeff wants someone using Clay from Claude Code to get about the same results. People should be able to use Clay wherever they already work. Usage is already much closer to a 50/50 split between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses than Jeff expected.  The push came from inside Clay. Its own go-to-market team lived in Cursor and wouldn’t leave it, so they asked for a CLI. The MCP team switched over to build it, and Clay’s sales team now does deal prep in Codex. So why build a first-party agent at all? Plenty of customers live in the Clay UI and want an agent right there. Jump to the agent platform discussion →Keep building when the plan blows up Jeff thinks it takes more courage to change plans at 600 people than it did at 50. Clay was a launch partner for ChatGPT apps. In the middle of the quarter, Clay put about a quarter of its engineers on the integration for a month. Two days before launch, OpenAI postponed it indefinitely. Clay kept building on the assumption that OpenAI would change its mind. Three or four days later, it did.  When Clay first showed customers Workflows, they were confused. Some were upset. They wanted their spreadsheet. Now agency owners like it, and a growing share of the work that used to run in tables runs in Workflows. Most workflows are built with the CLI or the agent. CEO Kareem Amin spent five years building Clay when almost nothing was working. Jeff still sees that persistence in the company today. Jump to the ChatGPT apps discussion →Agents still can't debug agents What Jeff wants most is a model that can read a long agent trace and tell him where the run went wrong. Today’s models tend to flag whichever step took a long time, even when the mistake was somewhere else. Clay would like to pull traces from bad runs, have an agent review them and use what it finds to improve the agent automatically. That still doesn’t work, and Clay writes a lot of its skills by hand.  Models still make basic mistakes, like retrying the same CLI command with the same inputs over and over. But when Jeff wanted to know how many YC companies use Clay, he asked the agent and had the answer in about a minute. A year ago, he would’ve had to scrape the batch, get access to Snowflake and cross-reference the two by hand. Jump to the agent debugging discussion →Show notesClay — the go-to-market platform where Jeff is Head of AI. Clay raises $115M to be the AI growth engine for every company — the September Series D at a $7.1 billion valuation, led by Wellington. Clay acquires Avenue to help growth teams act on intent signals — the January 2025 deal that brought Jeff's team to Clay. How Clay Scales GTM Agents — Jeff's LangChain Interrupt talk on running Clay's agents in production. Clay Agent Plugin (CLI & API) — the CLI and API that let Claude Code and Codex work directly with Clay. Inside Clay Workflows — how Workflows was built, including the table view customers asked to get back. Sellers have a new AI edge: Clay in ChatGPT — the ChatGPT app launch from Jeff's story. Sculpt recap: Building the self-learning revenue engine — Clay's October launches, including its new agent and Workflows. TypeSafe launched Jev because sequential LLMs are "totally useless for computers" — The New Stack on the classifier model behind Jeff's $1,500 math. items.content_html: Open video on YouTube ↗Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use. Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue, the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation. By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph. Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. Sculptor started as a tool loop. Now it's a coding agent. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings. The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows. Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together. Jump to the Sculptor discussion →Most companies post-train too early For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks. Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million. Jump to the post-training discussion →$1,500 to score every company in the world Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market. Jeff puts a good enrichment budget at $1 to $10 per qualified lead and $10 to $100 per booked call. He thinks qualification itself is close to solved. Models have been scoring about as high as they can on Clay’s evals for roughly a year. Just about any model from the past year can pull a company’s latest funding round. Frontier models still matter for deep prospecting research and for orchestration, where Jeff says the best plays can be ten to a hundred times as effective as an average one. Jump to the Jev discussion →Customers hate the model selector Customers complain when they see Clay’s model selector. They can’t check the evals for their use case every time a new model ships, and they shouldn’t have to. Clay is about to launch an automatic router that picks a model for each task. There’s no fancy branding. Finding Apple’s CEO is a very different job from finding the CEO of an obscure local company. The selector isn’t going away. Agency owners and power users still want control. Everyone else just wants to get on with their work. Clay has to earn their trust before they’ll leave it on auto. Jump to the model routing discussion →No Temporal, no LangGraph Clay built most of its agent stack itself. It uses BullMQ to keep agent jobs running, Postgres and ClickHouse for product data, and Snowflake for analytics. Jeff isn’t sure how BullMQ will hold up if usage grows another tenfold, but it’s held up so far. Clay recently shipped 25 to 30 new integrations. Contracts and testing took longer than the engineering work. Where Clay did run into trouble was scale. People run an agent per row, so if someone starts a run on a table of 50,000 companies, inference demand spikes all at once. Clay brought in LangSmith to see what was happening. The team also built a way to throttle requests and to pause and resume work when a provider goes down or starts rate-limiting. The harder part is keeping things fair. Someone running a workflow for ten people still needs it to run when an enterprise customer is enriching a million rows. Jump to the infrastructure discussion →Built for every agent, not just Clay's Clay plans to ship a sandboxed agent that’s free to use any of Clay’s tools and building blocks. Jeff wants someone using Clay from Claude Code to get about the same results. People should be able to use Clay wherever they already work. Usage is already much closer to a 50/50 split between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses than Jeff expected. The push came from inside Clay. Its own go-to-market team lived in Cursor and wouldn’t leave it, so they asked for a CLI. The MCP team switched over to build it, and Clay’s sales team now does deal prep in Codex. So why build a first-party agent at all? Plenty of customers live in the Clay UI and want an agent right there. Jump to the agent platform discussion →Keep building when the plan blows up Jeff thinks it takes more courage to change plans at 600 people than it did at 50. Clay was a launch partner for ChatGPT apps. In the middle of the quarter, Clay put about a quarter of its engineers on the integration for a month. Two days before launch, OpenAI postponed it indefinitely. Clay kept building on the assumption that OpenAI would change its mind. Three or four days later, it did. When Clay first showed customers Workflows, they were confused. Some were upset. They wanted their spreadsheet. Now agency owners like it, and a growing share of the work that used to run in tables runs in Workflows. Most workflows are built with the CLI or the agent. CEO Kareem Amin spent five years building Clay when almost nothing was working. Jeff still sees that persistence in the company today. Jump to the ChatGPT apps discussion →Agents still can't debug agents What Jeff wants most is a model that can read a long agent trace and tell him where the run went wrong. Today’s models tend to flag whichever step took a long time, even when the mistake was somewhere else. Clay would like to pull traces from bad runs, have an agent review them and use what it finds to improve the agent automatically. That still doesn’t work, and Clay writes a lot of its skills by hand. Models still make basic mistakes, like retrying the same CLI command with the same inputs over and over. But when Jeff wanted to know how many YC companies use Clay, he asked the agent and had the answer in about a minute. A year ago, he would’ve had to scrape the batch, get access to Snowflake and cross-reference the two by hand. Sculpt recap: Building the self-learning revenue engine — Clay's October launches, including its new agent and Workflows. items.content: Today, we’re releasing the open weights for OCRia-nano-1 , an extremely lightweight 8.1M-parameter model that brings fast, accurate document parsing to your local CPUs. We think it should be the default first pass for all document collections within your organization, even if the hardest documents require larger VLMs. And, we are releasing the full open weights on Hugging Face! LiteParse on GitHub : installation and usage. Nano on Hugging Face : model weights and license. Technical report : architecture, benchmarks and methodology. items.content:
The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites to process AI data as orbital data centers. SpaceX is targeting its first launches in 2027, and the full constellation is set to be operating by 2040. Google and Blue Origin are also working on AI infrastructure in space, but Boston Consulting Group estimates costs will stay well above ground-based data centers for now.

items.title: Your future housekeeper might be an XPeng
items.content: Your future housekeeper might be an XPeng PLUS: Amazon drone crashes trigger FAA scrutiny Jennifer Mossalgue , Rowan Cheung , Shubham Sharma & Zach Mink November 26, 2026 Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, robotics enthusiasts. China’s XPeng has unveiled an upgraded IRON humanoid that could greet car buyers by early 2027 — and tackle household chores a year or two after that. The move intensifies a race against Tesla, Figure AI, and a growing field of Chinese robotics companies looking to turn impressive humanoid demos into commercially useful machines, with the home robot as the ultimate prize. In today’s robotics rundown: XPeng’s humanoid has your home in its sights FAA probes Amazon’s Michigan drone crash Light-powered nanobots carry chemo into brains Zoox tests gentler robotaxi warnings LATEST DEVELOPMENTS XPENG 🤖 XPeng’s humanoid has your home in its sights Image source: XPeng (CEO He Xiaopeng) The Rundown: Chinese EV maker XPeng unveiled an updated IRON humanoid at its 2026 AI Day, targeting showroom work early next year as it sets its sights on robots that could eventually handle household chores. The details: IRON packs 76 degrees of freedom, 1,500+ tactile sensing points, and three Turing AI chips, with autonomous navigation and self-charging capabilities. XPeng targets mass production in January 2027, retail-assistant training in Q1, and a public release in Q2. Co-president Brian Gu told CNBC that home deployment could follow successful commercial use by one to two years, though no firm timeline has been set. XPeng is using the same AI architecture, VLA 3.0, to power both its humanoids and self-driving vehicles, including its YOYO-01 robotaxi, slated for 2027. Why it matters: XPeng is building IRON on the AI and data pipeline developed for its cars, but it’s chasing AgiBot and Unitree, which shipped ~16.7K humanoids in the first half of 2026. Homes also pose a tougher challenge than showrooms, with people often changing interiors and kids and pets running around. AMAZON 📦 FAA probes Amazon’s Michigan drone crash Image source: Amazon The Rundown: The FAA is reportedly investigating Amazon after a Prime Air drone dropped off a bottle of shampoo in a Detroit suburb, caught a fiber line on the way out, and ended up jammed against a neighbor’s garage roof. The details: Amazon’s MK30 drone reportedly hit a fiber-optic line on the climb, lost a propeller, and landed between a garage roof and an electrical cable. Amazon says the drone uses cameras and sensors to identify hazards, including power lines, and adjusts its flight when it detects an obstruction. The FAA is weighing corrective or enforcement action; the NTSB hasn’t decided whether to open a case. Waco, Texas, logged a similar strike last year, when an MK30 hit an internet line after a delivery and drew an FAA investigation. Why it matters: Amazon says Prime Air has delivered hundreds of thousands of packages in 2026, with nearly 6K flights daily. Still, similar collisions involving wires in Texas, a crane in Arizona, and an apartment building raise questions about how reliably its drones can navigate obstacles as deliveries scale up. NANOBOTS 🧠 Light-powered nanobots carry chemo into brains Image source: Gao Lab / Caltech The Rundown: Caltech researchers just said their light-activated BrainBots delivered about five times as much chemotherapy to mouse brains as unactivated carriers, potentially offering a new approach to getting drugs past the brain’s defenses. The details: Near-infrared light propels the 250nm carriers, as attached DNA molecules help them bind to cells that transport them across the blood–brain barrier. Eight hours after dosing, activated BrainBots delivered 5.2x as much doxorubicin to brain tissue as unactivated carriers, according to the researchers. In mice with glioblastoma, treatment slowed tumor growth and extended survival while reducing systemic toxicity compared with conventional methods. Oxford neuroscientist Tim Viney told the Financial Times that the tissue and neuroanatomical evidence needed “significant improvement” and questioned whether the approach could translate to humans. Why it matters: BrainBots join a growing field of experimental brain-delivery systems, including “ Trojanbots ” that use immune cells to carry chemotherapy-loaded nanobots toward brain tumors in mice. Another approach has already reached human trials: ultrasound and injected microbubbles to open the blood-brain barrier during chemo. ZOOX 🔊 Zoox tests gentler robotaxi warnings Image source: Zoox The Rundown: Zoox is building a street vocabulary for its robotaxis, starting with a better way to say “watch out.” In tests with Virginia Tech, custom warning tones warned would-be jaywalkers as reliably as a honking horn, without the jarring noise. The details: Forty participants, including 20 with low vision or visual impairments, completed 360 crossing trials: 200 midblock and 160 at marked crosswalks. The research vehicles featured

items.content: We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profitI’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford.If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people.The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. LingBot-Map 2.0 predicts camera poses and dense geometry from incoming RGB sequences. This repository provides the geometric streaming base model (without GCR) from the technical report, trained for causal Online Streaming. Streaming Reconstruction: Predict camera poses, intrinsics, depth and confidence from incoming RGB frames. Flexible Integration: Run reconstruction from the command line or integrate frame-by-frame inference and keyframe selection into your application. 📑 Table of Contents Click to expand Demo Video News TODO Installation Model Download Quick Start Interactive Demo ( demo.py ) Streaming Inference ( infer.py ) Benchmarks Resources License Citation Acknowledgments 📰 News 2026-11-23 — Added the evaluation benchmark with dataset preparation and evaluation instructions. 2026-11-21 — Released the causal streaming inference code. See Model Download for the geometric streaming base model. 📋 TODO ✅ Release model weights ✅ Release streaming inference code ✅ Release interactive demos and example sequences ✅ Release evaluation benchmarks ⚙️ Installation 1. Create a conda environment conda create -n lingbot-map2 python=3.11 -y
conda activate lingbot-map2 2. Install PyTorch (CUDA 12.8) A BF16-capable CUDA GPU and PyTorch 2.8 or later are required. For a CUDA 12.8 environment: pip install torch==2.8.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 3. Install the LingBot-Map 2.0 Geometric Streaming Base Model Clone or download this repository, then run from its root directory: pip install -e . FlashInfer is included in the package dependencies declared in pyproject.toml . If your package mirror does not carry it, install it with pip install --index-url https://pypi.org/simple flashinfer-python before installing this package. 4. Install benchmark dependencies (optional) pip install -e " .[benchmark] " 5. Install visualization dependencies (optional) pip install -e " .[vis] " 📦 Model Download Model Name Hugging Face ModelScope Description LingBot-Map 2.0 Geometric Streaming Base Model Hugging Face ModelScope Pure causal checkpoint for online 3D reconstruction. The model repositories are currently private. Authenticate with an
account that has access, then download the paired configuration and weights: pip install -U huggingface_hub
hf auth login
python download_model.py --source hf --output checkpoints/base-streaming For ModelScope, install modelscope , authenticate with a permitted account and
use --source modelscope . The downloader validates the weight SHA-256. Keep model_weights.pt and config.json together and pass both paths as shown below. The released configuration describes the Geometric Streaming Base Model checkpoint; causal.example.json is only a schema example. The loader checks the checkpoint SHA256, causal training mode, and every parameter key and shape. It accepts a model-only tensor dictionary or a model tensor dictionary loaded with weights_only=True . 🚀 Quick Start Run streaming reconstruction on a folder of RGB images: python infer.py \
    --checkpoint checkpoints/base-streaming/model_weights.pt \
    --config checkpoints/base-streaming/config.json \
    --images path/to/rgb \
    --output outputs/sequence Images are processed in natural filename order. The CLI retains Uniform320 keyframes while predicting every input frame; --keyframe-interval 1 retains every frame. Predictions include original raw_indices and are saved as .npz files containing poses, intrinsics, depth and confidence, alongside a run manifest. Use --image-list frames.json to supply an explicit input order. 🖥️ Interactive Demo ( demo.py ) View Online reconstruction in your browser with Viser : pip install -e " .[vis] " python demo.py \
    --checkpoint checkpoints/base-streaming/model_weights.pt \
    --config checkpoints/base-streaming/config.json \
    --images path/to/rgb --mask-sky Open http://localhost:8080 . The viewer mirrors LingBot-Map's interactive

direction , Reset Defaults , and Reset View Direction presets ( Look
At Scene Center , Overview , Front/Back/Top/Left/Right , First

items.title: Pangram is not an oracle • Buttondown
items.content: October 19, 2026 Pangram is not an oracle by Emily In light of Vauhini Vara's accusation that Simbarashe Kundizeza's Caine prize-winning story “ The Blue Fighter ” was generated with an LLM (see Kundizeza’s response here), I want to write a bit about how evaluation works in the field of natural language processing (NLP) and what claims of “accuracy” of systems mean for interpreting the output of a given tool on a particular input. Today's case in point is Pangram, a tool which has found many willing users in the publishing industry, but this applies to synthetic text detection tools more generally. I keep hearing Pangram described as extremely “accurate”. This tells me that a) the company’s advertising is effective and b) we need some public education on what “accuracy” means with respect to language technology and how such technologies are evaluated. This post is going to be primarily about evaluation practice, but the larger story isn’t—the larger story is about racism, about the use of software sold as “AI” to clothe racism in a veneer of objectivity, and the continuing demands placed on racialized authors, especially Black authors, to establish credibility to impossible standards. Others, such as Adio Dinika and Samantha Asumadu are better positioned to write about that broader story than I am, and I encourage you to read their words. I want to acknowledge that the synthetic media, including text, flooding our information ecosystem is a real problem. I have been writing about this for a while and we also write about it in The AI Con . But as always, we have to be wary of any proposed technical solutions and evaluate them with care (including asking whether a technical solution is called for at all). This is again one of those cases where machine learning can easily create something that looks like a solution, but isn't, because it's easy to make a machine that gives “scores” for how likely some text is to be synthetic/authentic. (If we had actually insisted on watermarking at the source, with large penalties for setting up non-watermarked systems for producing synthetic media, we'd live in a different world.) Key concept #1: Error type Synthetic text detection is a kind of text classification, where each input text is classified with one of two labels— synthetic (i.e., the text provided is the output of an LLM) or authentic (i.e., the text provided is something a person actually wrote). Generally speaking, the idea is to find synthetic text so it can be removed and/or so its purported author can be censured (or, in the case of prior authors accused of using LLMs, denied book contracts ). Given that framing, calling something authentic when it's actually synthetic is a false negative (the system allowed synthetic text to slip through) and calling something synthetic when it's actually authentic is a false positive (this system is used to accuse someone of using an LLM when they didn’t). Accuracy, on the other hand, measures how many labels were correct as a proportion of all the predicted labels. In mathematical terms, it is the number of true positives and true negatives divided by everything fed into the models (that is, true positives plus false positives plus true negatives plus false negatives). To get a sense of how well a language processing system is working, you need to look at both the false negative rate and the false positive rate. Looking at just overall accuracy could be misleading—it will depend heavily on the true positive rate in the test data. Similarly, looking at just false positives or false negatives is also misleading, because there is always a trade-off. Want something that has no false negatives? Design the system to always return “synthetic”. Want no false positives? Always return “authentic”. In this context, it is disingenuous that Pangram (whose software is advertised as “An AI detector that actually works”) presents “case studies” on its website looking only at false negatives : False negative-only reporting or only at false postives : False positive-only reporting This one is also especially suspect, since they report 0 false positives. As is widely known within the NLP research community, perfect results usually point to something wrong with the evaluation setup. For instance, an experiment may have not been constructed correctly, or you may have ruined the evaluation experiment by allowing test data to contaminate training data. Also, appallingly, the Pangram website hosts a case study with the headline “AI is Writing Prize-Winning Fiction.” That headline is substantiated ... only by Pangram scores over specific pieces. Bold assertions based on Pangram output No other corroborating information is provided. items.content_html: October 19, 2026 Pangram is not an oracle by Emily In light of Vauhini Vara's accusation that Simbarashe Kundizeza's Caine prize-winning story “ The Blue Fighter ” was generated with an LLM (see Kundizeza’s response here), I want to write a bit about how evaluation works in the field of natural language processing (NLP) and what claims of “accuracy” of systems mean for interpreting the output of a given tool on a particular input. Today's case in point is Pangram, a tool which has found many willing users in the publishing industry, but this applies to synthetic text detection tools more generally. I keep hearing Pangram described as extremely “accurate”. This tells me that a) the company’s advertising is effective and b) we need some public education on what “accuracy” means with respect to language technology and how such technologies are evaluated. This post is going to be primarily about evaluation practice, but the larger story isn’t—the larger story is about racism, about the use of software sold as “AI” to clothe racism in a veneer of objectivity, and the continuing demands placed on racialized authors, especially Black authors, to establish credibility to impossible standards. Others, such as Adio Dinika and Samantha Asumadu are better positioned to write about that broader story than I am, and I encourage you to read their words. I want to acknowledge that the synthetic media, including text, flooding our information ecosystem is a real problem. I have been writing about this for a while and we also write about it in The AI Con . But as always, we have to be wary of any proposed technical solutions and evaluate them with care (including asking whether a technical solution is called for at all). This is again one of those cases where machine learning can easily create something that looks like a solution, but isn't, because it's easy to make a machine that gives “scores” for how likely some text is to be synthetic/authentic. (If we had actually insisted on watermarking at the source, with large penalties for setting up non-watermarked systems for producing synthetic media, we'd live in a different world.) Key concept #1: Error type Synthetic text detection is a kind of text classification, where each input text is classified with one of two labels— synthetic (i.e., the text provided is the output of an LLM) or authentic (i.e., the text provided is something a person actually wrote). Generally speaking, the idea is to find synthetic text so it can be removed and/or so its purported author can be censured (or, in the case of prior authors accused of using LLMs, denied book contracts ). Given that framing, calling something authentic when it's actually synthetic is a false negative (the system allowed synthetic text to slip through) and calling something synthetic when it's actually authentic is a false positive (this system is used to accuse someone of using an LLM when they didn’t). Accuracy, on the other hand, measures how many labels were correct as a proportion of all the predicted labels. In mathematical terms, it is the number of true positives and true negatives divided by everything fed into the models (that is, true positives plus false positives plus true negatives plus false negatives). To get a sense of how well a language processing system is working, you need to look at both the false negative rate and the false positive rate. Looking at just overall accuracy could be misleading—it will depend heavily on the true positive rate in the test data. Similarly, looking at just false positives or false negatives is also misleading, because there is always a trade-off. Want something that has no false negatives? Design the system to always return “synthetic”. Want no false positives? Always return “authentic”. In this context, it is disingenuous that Pangram (whose software is advertised as “An AI detector that actually works”) presents “case studies” on its website looking only at false negatives : False negative-only reporting or only at false postives : False positive-only reporting This one is also especially suspect, since they report 0 false positives. As is widely known within the NLP research community, perfect results usually point to something wrong with the evaluation setup. For instance, an experiment may have not been constructed correctly, or you may have ruined the evaluation experiment by allowing test data to contaminate training data. Also, appallingly, the Pangram website hosts a case study with the headline “AI is Writing Prize-Winning Fiction.” That headline is substantiated ... only by Pangram scores over specific pieces. items.title: AI Test Case Generation for Production QA Pipelines
items.content:
Code production is speeding up: CI/CD pipelines deliver frequent code changes, and AI coding tools can increase the volume of generated code. But with more code comes higher testing demand, and manually creating and updating test cases becomes a common bottleneck.AI test case generation addresses this by reducing repetitive test design work. This article explores how LLM test generation works and how to incorporate AI-generated tests into QA pipelines.What AI test case generation automatesAI test case generation automatically creates candidate test cases based on an application’s intended behavior. AI analyzes inputs, like natural-language user prompts and software requirements, and identifies scenarios worth testing. The output specifies what teams should test, under which conditions, and what results to expect.AI test automation helps teams keep up with the pace of frequent software changes by proposing or updating relevant regression testing scenarios, suggesting edge case scenarios, and reducing manual test design. It can also expand test coverage by identifying potentially overlooked scenarios.How AI-generated test cases workA schematic diagram illustrating the AI-assisted test generation: source data is submitted to an AI agent; a structured output with a test description is converted into an actual script within testing frameworks; CI/CD pipelines execute the pre-generated test scriptsThe AI test case generation process includes:Providing application information like prompts, requirements, source code, or user flowsGenerating test scenarios including test steps, conditions, and expected resultsValidating the outputs for format, completeness, and correctnessConverting to executable scripts translates the validated, structured test steps into actual automation code (such as PyTest, Jest, or Playwright) that a test runner can execute Executing through a testing workflow, involves running test cases, collecting and reporting resultsHere’s a closer look.Prompt-driven test generationTo turn written requirements into test cases, teams provide the model with instructions describing what to test and relevant application requirements, and sometimes include examples or expected output format. Models use the context to interpret the requested functionality and identify behaviors or conditions worth testing, generating test cases containing conditions, steps, and expected outcomes. The clearer the requirements and expected test-case format, the more relevant and accurate the AI-generated tests. Ambiguous acceptance criteria can cause the model to invent assumptions or produce tests that don’t match the intended functionality. Behavioral and workflow analysisIn addition to prompt-driven generation, AI can develop and update tests using provided application information. Potential inputs might include recorded user interactions and workflows, application logs and past test results, UI designs, and application changes. Analyzing sequences of interactions helps AI identify alternative user paths, missing checks, and potential failure conditions. Structured output and validationAI can output test cases as an unstructured paragraph, but it’s also possible to request a more consistent, structured output such as a JSON object with fields like test_name, precondition, steps, and expected_result. In addition to allowing downstream systems to process tests predictably, structured output directly supports validation. A JSON schema can check whether generated output has required fields and whether those fields contain the expected data types. A separate requirements-based validation check evaluates whether the generated steps and expected results match the application’s requirements. This may require human review.💡In n8n, teams can perform schema checks with the Structured Output Parser.Common use cases for AI test case generationAI-generated test cases support different types of testing throughout the software development lifecycle. Here are four of the most common use cases. AI agents can generate tests for various frameworks, be it unit tests, API or E2E testing automationsRegression testingRegression testing is one of the most repetitive tasks for QA teams, requiring checks after every code change, issue fix, and update. AI can introduce more efficiency by suggesting new or updated regression scenarios based on:Code and application changes: To identify affected componentsApplication requirements: To establish intended behaviorExisting tests: To show what’s already coveredHistorical defects and test results: To identify previous problematic areasSome AI tools can prioritize tests based on what was changed. Teams dealing with large regression suites can run the most relevant tests first and receive feedback on potentially affected functionality. For example, when introducing an updated discount calculation for an e-commerce system, AI might suggest test scenarios to ensure it doesn’t affect existing promotional codes or shipping charges.API testingAPIs accept many different parameters, payloads, and authentication conditions, requiring testing to verify how an endpoint responds to different combinations of inputs. AI can use API specifications, endpoint descriptions, and request schemas to suggest test inputs and expected responses. This is useful for scenarios such as valid requests, missing required fields, incorrect data types, invalid authentication, and boundary values. For an API endpoint that lets users retrieve account details, for instance, AI could generate test cases for a valid authentication token, an expired token, or a missing token.E2E testingEnd-to-end (E2E) testing involves multiple elements, states, and possible paths, each requiring testing. AI analyzes UI designs, recorded interactions, and application flows to propose tests for different user behaviors. Useful scenarios include form validation, navigation, error messages, interrupted processes, and multi-step transactions.For an online checkout process, AI might generate test cases like completing a purchase successfully, entering an invalid shipping address, or abandoning checkout.CI/CD and automated QA pipelinesModern CI/CD pipelines involve frequent commits and releases, requiring testing to keep up with the pace of development. AI can help by producing or updating test cases based on new requirements, pull requests, or code changes. Teams can focus on validating AI-generated test cases, converting them to executable tests when needed, and adding them to automated testing processes. Let’s say a developer opens a pull request containing changes to how declined payments are handled. An AI system could propose tests for the updated functionality. The QA system or reviewer would first validate the tests for structure, correctness, and execution readiness. They might check that the tests match the acceptance criteria; in this case, that a declined payment doesn’t result in a paid order. Once validated, the tests can be run as part of the CI pipeline, with results reported before the change is merged.Where workflow orchestration fits into AI testing automationGenerating test cases with AI is just the first step in the testing process. AI-generated test cases move through multiple systems before they can contribute to AI software testing, including LLMs, validation tools, testing frameworks, and CI/CD platforms. Workflow orchestration coordinates these stages and tools, manages dependencies, and helps ensure failures are handled appropriately. n8n is an AI-native, source-available workflow automation platform that manages that coordination. n8n combines AI capabilities, API integrations, and customizable automation logic. It helps coordinate the different stages of AI QA automation, from automated test case generation and validation to execution and monitoring.

Coordinating AI-generated test workflowsWorkflow coordination determines the order of operations and conditions under which AI-assisted testing workflows continue. n8n workflows consist of connected visual nodes that can retrieve, process, or send data and be combined into automated processes. An AI-generated test workflow can be triggered by multiple things: a software change, a CI/CD event, or a new testing request. Nodes then perform operations such as retrieving requirements or sending data to an AI model. n8n’s AI Agent node lets an LLM select and use connected tools, such as choosing which sources to consult when gathering context for test generation. AI-generated test cases pass through structural checks and requirements-based review as necessary. Validation and conditional logic determine which operations run next. The workflow then passes approved outputs to a downstream system such as a testing framework or external runner.Monitoring execution and failuresWorkflow orchestration enables teams to track what happens during automated testing and respond when something goes wrong. n8n’s Executions list lets teams view workflow runs to identify failed or problematic executions. Teams can also debug by loading data from previous executions into a workflow, making it easier to reproduce and investigate problems. This feature is available on all Cloud plans and self-hosted Business, Enterprise, and Community.When a workflow execution fails, error workflows trigger alerts or other configured responses. The Error Trigger receives information such as the failure message and the last node executed, so teams know which operation failed. For a big picture view, n8n’s Evaluations test the workflow itself. This ensures the test-generation stage still produces reliable output when prompts or AI models change.Orchestrating integrations across testing systemsTesting workflows typically involve issue trackers, AI providers, source code repositories, CI/CD platforms, and test runners. n8n provides the connections needed to move information and trigger operations across these otherwise separate applications and tools. n8n initiates various tests and the AI Agent node prepares reports and groups related failures to reduce the number of backlog items in the issue-tracking toolThe Webhook node receives data from external applications when an event occurs, triggering a workflow. For example, a CI/CD platform could send an event when a new build is ready for testing. The HTTP Request node sends HTTP requests to external services if they don’t have a dedicated integration. For workflows that have already generated and validated a set of tests, the HTTP Request node can call an external testing service’s API to initiate a test run. Once the service executes the tests, n8n can receive or retrieve the results, depending on how the service’s API works.

Thanksgiving is here, and for many of us, that means plenty of catching up around the dinner table. If the conversation goes anything like the news cycle, AI may be a main course. Last year, that might’ve meant explaining ChatGPT to a relative. This year, the questions are about the Chinese spy saga, everything being hacked, data centers, and more. Choose your seat wisely! My brain said no way. I ran a software company for photographers, and we hosted terabytes of their images. A freeze frame every second of a three-hour game? items.content_html: Home Posts Your AI cheat sheet for Thanksgiving dinner Your AI cheat sheet for Thanksgiving dinner PLUS: Use Gemini Tasks to hunt for Black Friday prices Nov 26, 2026 Zach Mink , Rowan Cheung , Shubham Sharma & Jennifer Mossalgue Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,638 new readers. Thanksgiving is here, and for many of us, that means plenty of catching up around the dinner table. If the conversation goes anything like the news cycle, AI may be a main course. Last year, that might’ve meant explaining ChatGPT to a relative. This year, the questions are about the Chinese spy saga, everything being hacked, data centers, and more. Choose your seat wisely! In today’s AI rundown: Your AI cheat sheet for Thanksgiving dinner What five cents builds now with AI Check Black Friday prices with Gemini Tasks Anthropic CEO claps back at Axios ‘free will’ report LATEST DEVELOPMENTS AI & THE HOLIDAYS 🦃 Your AI cheat sheet for Thanksgiving dinner Image source: Images 2.6 / The Rundown The Rundown: AI is probably going to come up in discussion around the table during the holidays, and this month provided plenty of material. Here’s your cheat sheet for some of the questions most likely to get dished out, with explanations to help you feel like the AI expert in the room. Q: What’s going on with Nvidia and Jensen Huang? Was he really having an affair with a spy? A: Jensen was out, and now he’s back, with some lobbying from the President playing a role. Nvidia’s stock saw $1T in value added on his return, and lawmakers are furious — and ready to hold his feet to the fire in hearings starting on Dec. 3. As for his affair with Alice Huang, her spy ties are looking less clear by the day. Despite early reporting, U.S. officials reportedly have no proof she was told to pry secrets from Jensen, though she was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The bigger issue is chips: investigators suspect her old firm Megaspeed helped Nvidia hardware slip into China, and the U.S. blacklisted it Monday. Q: Why does it feel like everything’s getting hacked or breaking lately? Is AI to blame? A: Sort of — but it’s also the solution. AI is now extremely adept at finding bugs that sat unnoticed in everyday software for a decade or more. The code behind much of the web, including critical software and infrastructure, is not as safe as we once thought, and defenders are racing (with their own AI) to find and patch the holes. Unfortunately, expect more chaos, as more AI-exposed vulnerabilities seem inevitable at this point. Q: Did AI really solve some famous math problem? A: Yes, many of them. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others are all letting AI loose on the math world, solving open problems in the field left and right and igniting a firestorm between mathematicians and the AI labs. The biggest: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge claimed last week that he and Claude solved the Riemann Hypothesis, a $1M Millennium Prize problem considered the most famous open problem in mathematics. Also historic was OpenAI's Navier-Stokes solution in September and its release of 700+ AI-written math papers in October. TOGETHER WITH STRIPE 🔎 23,000 startups, three clear shifts The Rundown: 2025 startups on Stripe Atlas' median six-month revenue rose 39% versus 2024. Here’s how: Faster customers: 20% took payments within 30 days Selling globally from day one: Top 10% reached 15 countries within six months AI agent focus: 42% of new C corps build AI products, especially agents Get the report . NATE’S NOTEBOOK 🪙 What five cents builds now with AI The Rundown: Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he's seeing while teaching real teams to use AI. Nate: Live sports is the one place we all still sit through loud, annoying ads. My wife yells, “God, turn it down,” and I’m digging for the remote. One Saturday, it hit me: I could take a picture every second of what’s on my TV. If my Mac could look at each one and answer one question — game or ad — the TV could mute itself. My brain said no way. I ran a software company for photographers, and we hosted terabytes of their images. A freeze frame every second of a three-hour game? I figured $10 or $20 a game, fine for a funny proof of concept. It took under 30 minutes to build. It was 95% accurate on the first try. The cost? 5 cents a game. Then the snowball started. Once it could mute the ads, I thought about what I do during them: grab my phone and scroll for funny posts to send my buddies. So those went up on the TV. Then I swapped my feed for agents reading the top channels across every network, putting the best 20 posts on screen for the whole family to laugh at. I even swapped the TV announcers for the radio broadcast. Advertisers are not ready for this. My experience is my biggest asset, and it’s also my biggest blind spot: I keep assuming complexity and costs that aren’t there.
